RAZI-FULL:v17p59#2/r4.anchor: وصار العناء الشديد الذي تحمله في الماضي سببا لحصول الشقاء الشديد له في المستقبل

RAZI-FULL:v17p59#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v17p59#2/r5.speaker: القاضي
RAZI-FULL:v17p59#2/r5.claim: A fifth analogy addresses deniers of resurrection: as a barren-looking earth can become adorned again, the one able to renew it can restore the dead and recompense their deeds.
RAZI-FULL:v17p59#2/r5.anchor: فذكر هذا المثال ليدل عل أن من قدر على ذلك ، كان قادرا على إعادة الأحياء

ASAD-NOTES:10:24#n38/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:10:24#n38/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:10:24#n38/r1.claim: The dwellers' supposed mastery means mastery over nature without perceived limits to future achievement.
ASAD-NOTES:10:24#n38/r1.anchor: they come to believe that they have gained "mastery over nature", with no conceivable limits to what they may yet achieve

ASAD-NOTES:10:24#n38/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:10:24#n38/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:10:24#n38/r2.claim: Asad reads the adornment as artificial and illusory, produced by technology in hostile confrontation with nature rather than in cooperation with it.
ASAD-NOTES:10:24#n38/r2.anchor: the artificial, illusory "adornment" brought about by man's technological efforts, not in collaboration with nature but, rather

ASAD-NOTES:10:24#n39/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:10:24#n39/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:10:24#n39/r1.claim: The phrase means that the field had entirely disappeared or perished, a classical Arabic idiom.
ASAD-NOTES:10:24#n39/r1.anchor: a phrase used in classical Arabic to describe something that has entirely disappeared or perished

STUDYQURAN:10:24/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r1.claim: The parable follows the mention of worldly life in v. 23 and stresses its evanescence, alongside related parables in 29:64 and 18:45.
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r1.anchor: After the mention of the life of this world in v. 23, v. 24 lays down a parable that draws attention to its evanescent nature

STUDYQURAN:10:24/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r2.speaker: al-Rāzī
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r2.claim: The verse addresses people deluded by worldly life who have no concern for the Hereafter.
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r2.anchor: Al-Rāzī notes that this verse is aimed at those who are deluded by this world

STUDYQURAN:10:24/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r3.claim: Rain rejuvenates the earth and produces diverse vegetation; this growth is the earth taking on luster and becoming adorned.
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r3.anchor: When rain descends from the sky, the earth is rejuvenated and from it many different types of vegetation spring forth

STUDYQURAN:10:24/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r4.claim: The colorful herbage and varied benefits of the garden delight its inhabitants.
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r4.anchor: With its beautiful herbage and color, the earth’s garden brings delight to its inhabitants because of the multifarious ways in which they can benefit from it

STUDYQURAN:10:24/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r5.speaker: Kl, N, R, Z
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r5.claim: The Command that destroys the garden is understood as a violent wind, torrent, or mighty blast.
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r5.anchor: God’s Command, here understood to be a violent wind, torrent, or some kind of mighty blast (Kl, N, R, Z)

STUDYQURAN:10:24/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r6.speaker: Th
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r6.claim: The Command’s arrival by night or day means it can come at any moment.
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r6.anchor: by night or by day—that is, at any moment (Th)

STUDYQURAN:10:24/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r7.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r7.claim: The Command obliterates the garden’s trees and vegetation, leaving it like a mown field.
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r7.anchor: thereby obliterating its trees and vegetation (R), leaving the garden as a mown field

STUDYQURAN:10:24/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r8.speaker: al-Rāzī
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r8.claim: One who invests the heart in worldly pleasures suffers immense sorrow and grief when those pleasures leave.
STUDYQURAN:10:24/r8.anchor: This verse prompts al-Rāzī to observe, “Such is the one who invests his heart in the pleasures of this world

TAB-FULL:v12p150/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r1.claim: The worldly life and its wealth and adornment, dulled by loss and death, resemble rain that produces mixed vegetation for people and animals.
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r1.anchor: إنما مثل ما تباهون في الدنيا وتفاخرون به من زينتها وأموالها مع ما قد وكل بذلك من التكدير والتنغيص وزواله بالفناء والموت

TAB-FULL:v12p150/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the rain grows every kind of plant: grain, legumes, and fruit for people, and grasses and pasture for livestock.
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r2.anchor: كالحنطة والشعير وسائر حبوب الأرض والبقول والثمار

TAB-FULL:v12p150/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r3.claim: The earth's taking its adornment means its beauty appears; its owners think they control what it has grown, but God's decree destroys it by night or day and leaves it cut down.

TAB-FULL:v12p150/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r4.claim: The crops seem to have never existed; the root of تغن means to dwell or remain, as al-Nābigha's verse illustrates, just as worldly splendor vanishes.
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r4.anchor: وأصله: من غني فلان بمكان كذا، يغنى به: إذا أقام به

TAB-FULL:v12p150/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r5.claim: God explains signs for reflective people because they distinguish matters and investigate the realities behind doubts.
TAB-FULL:v12p150/r5.anchor: وخص به أهل الفكر، لأنهم أهل التمييز بين الأمور والفحص عن حقائق ما يعرض من الشبه

TAB-FULL:v12p152/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r1.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r1.claim: Qatada warns that people who cling to worldly life will soon be cast off and undone by it.
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r1.anchor: لئن تشبث بالدنيا وحدب عليها لتوشكن الدنيا أن تلفظه وتقضي منه

TAB-FULL:v12p152/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r2.claim: Qatada glosses وازينت as the earth having sprouted and become beautiful.

TAB-FULL:v12p152/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says Ubayy ibn Kaʿb taught an added reading that the earth would not be destroyed except for its people's sins; the phrase is absent from the codex.
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r3.anchor: فقال عباس بن عبد الله بن العباس: هكذا يقرؤها ابن عباس

TAB-FULL:v12p152/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r4.speaker: أبو سلمة بن عبد الرحمن
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r4.claim: Abu Salama reports Ubayy's reading with the added explanation that God destroyed the land only because of its people's sins.
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r4.anchor: {كأن لم تغن بالأمس} [يونس: 24] وما أهلكناها إلا بذنوب أهلها

TAB-FULL:v12p152/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r5.claim: Most readers pronounce وازينت as تزينت, assimilating tā into zā and adding a connecting alif; some read وأزينت, but al-Ṭabarī prefers the majority reading by reader consensus.
TAB-FULL:v12p152/r5.anchor: والصواب من القراءة في ذلك: {وازينت} [يونس: 24] لإجماع الحجة من القراء عليها

TABATABAI:10:23-25/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:10:23-25/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:10:23-25/r2.claim: Worldly life is illustrated through a sustained representational analogy of rain and flourishing vegetation, not a simple one-to-one comparison of isolated things.
TABATABAI:10:23-25/r2.anchor: وهو من الاستعادة التمثيلية وليس من تشبيه المفرد بالمفرد من شيء

TABATABAI:10:23-25/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:10:23-25/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:10:23-25/r3.claim: Al-zukhruf means ornament and beauty; lam taghn means that a place remained settled there for a long time.
TABATABAI:10:23-25/r3.anchor: من غني في المكان إذا أقام فيه فأطال المقام

TABRISI:10:24-25/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r1.speaker: الأعرج، الشعبي، أبو العالية، نصر بن عاصم، الحسن
TABRISI:10:24-25/r1.claim: In anomalous readings, these readers read وأزينت, with the attribution to al-Hasan qualified as disputed.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r1.anchor: قراءة الأعرج والشعبي وأبي العالية ونصر بن عاصم والحسن بخلاف وأزينت

TABRISI:10:24-25/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r2.speaker: أبو عثمان
TABRISI:10:24-25/r2.claim: Abu Uthman is reported to read وازيأنت.

TABRISI:10:24-25/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r3.claim: The form ازينت derives from تزينت by assimilating ta into zay, then taking a connecting alif after the now vowelless zay.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r3.anchor: أما ازينت فأصله تزينت فأدغمت التاء في الزاي وسكنت الزاي

TABRISI:10:24-25/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r4.claim: أزينت follows the form أفعلت, meaning that the earth came with adornment; the related إزينت is better Arabic, with the preferable form أزانت, like أقال and أ clockباع.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r4.anchor: وأما أزينت فإنه على أفعلت أي جاءت بالزينة وإزينت أجود في العربية

TABRISI:10:24-25/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r5.claim: أزيأنت follows أفعالت and derives from أزيانت; a disliked meeting of two vowelless letters turns the alif into hamza, as in the cited line's ادهامت.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r5.anchor: وأما أزيأنت فوزنه أفعالت وأصله أزيانت مثل ادهامت واسوادت

TABRISI:10:24-25/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r6.claim: The line by Kathir is cited as evidence for the form ادهامت.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r6.anchor: كقول كثير: وللأرض أما سودها فتجللت بياضا وأما بيضها فأدهامت

TABRISI:10:24-25/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r7.claim: Zukhruf means the fullest beauty of a thing; decorating it means making it beautiful, and the phrase about Paradise describes its finest colors.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r7.anchor: الزخرف: كمال حسن الشيء. ويقال زخرفته أي حسنته

TABRISI:10:24-25/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r8.claim: The verb غني بالمكان means to reside there, and المغاني means dwellings; al-Nabigha's line witnesses غنيت in this sense.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r8.anchor: وغني بالمكان أقام به والمغاني المنازل قال النابغة:

TABRISI:10:24-25/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r9.claim: A supplication requests an action for its purpose, while a caller to action opposes the deterrent from acting.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r9.anchor: والدعاء طلب الفعل بما يقع لأجله والداعي إلى الفعل خلاف الصارف عنه

TABRISI:10:24-25/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r10.claim: Both command and supplication request action, but command encourages doing it and warns against leaving it, has a recognized form, and presumes the addressee is lower in rank; supplication does not.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r10.anchor: والفرق بين الدعاء الأمر أن في الأمر ترغيبا في الفعل وزجرا عن تركه وله صيغة

TABRISI:10:24-25/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r11.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r11.claim: The worldly-life simile follows exhortation toward the afterlife and disinterest in this world, contrasting the conditions of the two abodes.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r11.anchor: لما تقدم ما يوجب الترغيب في الآخرة والتزهيد في الدنيا عقبه سبحانه بذكر صفة الدارين

TABRISI:10:24-25/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r12.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r12.claim: The simile compares worldly life to rain in the benefit it gives before its interruption and disappearance.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r12.anchor: أنه تعالى شبه الحياة الدنيا بالماء فيما يكون به من الانتفاع ثم الانقطاع

TABRISI:10:24-25/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r13.speaker: الجبائي، أبو مسلم
TABRISI:10:24-25/r13.claim: Al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim are reported to say that worldly life is like the plants described, which first deceive and then vanish.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r13.anchor: أنه شبهها بالنبات على ما وصفه من الاغترار به ثم المصير إلى الزوال عن الجبائي وأبي مسلم

TABRISI:10:24-25/r14.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r14.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r14.claim: A third reported comparison makes worldly life like a life stipulated to have these very qualities.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r14.anchor: شبه الحياة الدنيا بحياة مقدرة على هذه الأوصاف

TABRISI:10:24-25/r15.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r15.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r15.claim: Rain enters the spaces within plants and mixes with them; alternatively, rain causes different plants to mingle, including human food with animal fodder and staple crops with fruit.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r15.anchor: لأن المطر يدخل في خلل النبات فيختلط به

TABRISI:10:24-25/r16.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r16.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r16.claim: Human food includes grains, fruit, and vegetables, while animal food includes grass and other kinds of pasture.

TABRISI:10:24-25/r17.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r17.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r17.claim: The earth takes on beauty and splendor through its varied colors and kinds of plants.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r17.anchor: أي حسنها وبهجتها بأنواع الألوان وأجناس النبات وغير ذلك

TABRISI:10:24-25/r18.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r18.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r18.claim: Its people are its owners; they think they can benefit from its produce because it seems ready to harvest, yield, or preserve.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r18.anchor: أي مالكها { أنهم قادرون عليها } أي

TABRISI:10:24-25/r19.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r19.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r19.claim: The sudden command is explained either as a destructive cold or hail, or as God's decree and judgment to destroy and ruin it.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r19.anchor: أي أتاها عذابنا من برد أو برد

TABRISI:10:24-25/r20.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25/r20.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25/r20.claim: The crop is cut down, uprooted, gone, and dry, as though it had not stood in that condition the previous day or existed before.
TABRISI:10:24-25/r20.anchor: أي محصودة ومعناه مقطوعة مقلوعة ذاهبة يابسة

TABRISI:10:24-25#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25#2/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25#2/r1.claim: God distinguishes the signs in this way for people who reflect and take instruction from them.
TABRISI:10:24-25#2/r1.anchor: مثل ذلك نميز الآيات لقوم يتفكرون فيها فيعتبرون بها

TABRISI:10:24-25#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:10:24-25#2/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:10:24-25#2/r2.claim: Worldly life ends at death just as plants perish through calamities; the warning encourages people to expect its end and avoid being deceived by its conditions.
TABRISI:10:24-25#2/r2.anchor: الدنيا تنقطع وتفنى بالموت كما يفنى هذا النبات بفنون الآفات

THALABI:v5p127/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p127/r5.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p127/r5.claim: The worldly life is like rain that mingles with earth’s plants: people eat grains, vegetables, and fruits, while livestock graze on herbage.
THALABI:v5p127/r5.anchor: كماء أنزلناه من السماء فاختلط به نبات الأرض مما يأكل الناس من الحبوب

THALABI:v5p127/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p127/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p127/r6.claim: The common reading is wa-zzayyanat; Ibn Masʿud’s reading wa-tazayyanat confirms the sense that the earth becomes adorned.
THALABI:v5p127/r6.anchor: وازينت هذا قراءة العامة، وتصديقها قراءة عبد الله بن مسعود: وتزينت

THALABI:v5p127/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p127/r7.speaker: أبو عثمان النهدي والضحاك
THALABI:v5p127/r7.claim: Abu Uthman al-Nahdi and al-Dahhak read wāzānat on the pattern of ajāzat; ʿAwf says their elders read it likewise.
THALABI:v5p127/r7.anchor: وقرأ أبو عثمان النهدي والضحاك: وازانت على وزن اجازت

THALABI:v5p127/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p127/r8.speaker: أبو رجاء وأبو العالية والشعبي والحسن والأعرج
THALABI:v5p127/r8.claim: These readers pronounce wa-zzayyanat with a separated hamza and light form; Qutrub glosses it as bringing forth its adornment.
THALABI:v5p127/r8.anchor: وقرأ أبو رجاء وأبو العالية والشعبي والحسن والأعرج: وازينت على وزن أفعلت

THALABI:v5p127/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p127/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p127/r9.claim: Although the verse says the earth thinks it can control its produce, the pronoun is explained as the plants, the harvest, or the adornment.
THALABI:v5p127/r9.anchor: أخبر عن الأرض ويعني للنبات إذ كان مفهوما وقيل: رده إلى الغلة

THALABI:v5p127/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p127/r10.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p127/r10.claim: God’s command means His decree of destruction; ḥaṣīd describes crops cut down and uprooted.
THALABI:v5p127/r10.anchor: أتاها أمرنا قضاؤنا بهلاكها ليلا أو نهارا

THALABI:v5p127/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p127/r11.speaker: author
THALABI:v5p127/r11.claim: The phrase ka-an lam taghn means the land had not remained inhabited; its root refers to a place where someone stayed and built.
THALABI:v5p127/r11.anchor: كأن لم تغن تكن، وأصله من غني المكان إذا أقام فيه وعمره،

THALABI:v5p127/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v5p127/r12.speaker: قتادة
THALABI:v5p127/r12.claim: The common reading has feminine taghn referring to the earth, while Qatada reads yaghn with the masculine referent al-zukhruf.
THALABI:v5p127/r12.anchor: وقرأها العامة: تغن بالتاء لتأنيث الأرض، وقرأها قتادة بالياء

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p127/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p127/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p127/r1.claim: To detail the signs is to explain them; the people who know are those who infer God's power from indicators and proofs, unlike the ignorant.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p127/r1.anchor: أي يتدلون بالأمارات والبراهين على قدرة الله

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r1.claim: The parable compares the condition of worldly life to the described water, or means its quality is like water; worldly life here is the transient life of this world.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r1.anchor: وأراد بالحياة الدنيا الحياة الفانية في هذه الدار

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r2.claim: The water makes the earth's plants intermingle: people eat vegetables, grains, and fruits, while livestock graze on pasture.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r2.anchor: فاختلط -بسبب ذلك الماء الذي أنزلناه- نبات الأرض

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says the earth taking its adornment means its beauty and fertility; al-Zajjaj calls it complete beauty, while another view refers to the pleasing colors of flowers.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r4.claim: The source links the word zukhru f to its earlier discussion in 6:112, where it occurs in 'adorned speech'.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163/r4.anchor: ومضى الكلام في معنى الزخرف عند قوله: {زخرف القول غرورا}

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says 'adorned' refers to grain and fruit; another view refers to the plants themselves.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r2.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r2.claim: Al-Zajjaj derives izzayyanat from tazayyanat by assimilating ta into zay and adding a joining alif; he compares 2:72 and 7:38.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says the land's people thought they could harvest, gather, and cut its crops; al-Zajjaj says they thought they could benefit from it.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r4.speaker: أهل المعاني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r4.claim: Although the pronoun refers grammatically to the earth, the intended referent is its plants; another account takes it as the crop because context implies it.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r4.anchor: أخبر عن الأرض، والمعنى للنبات إذ كان مفهوما

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says God's command coming to the land means His punishment, that is, the command to destroy it.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p163#2/r5.anchor: {أتاها أمرنا}، قال ابن عباس: يريد عذابنا

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas explains 'made it harvested' as leaving nothing there; al-Dahhak takes it as the harvested crop, while Abu Ubayda says completely uprooted and another view says cut or pulled out.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r1.anchor: قال ابن عباس: لا شيء فيها (¬2). وقال الضحاك

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r2.speaker: الليث
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r2.claim: Al-Layth explains 'as if it had not flourished yesterday' as having vanished, from the verb for a people residing in their home; Ibn Abbas similarly says it was as if it had not existed.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r2.anchor: يقال للشيء إذا فني: كأن لم يغن بالأمس

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r3.speaker: الزجاج
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r3.claim: Al-Zajjaj says it was as if the land had not been inhabited yesterday; Ibn Qutayba agrees, so this reading refers to the land rather than its produce.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r3.anchor: كأن لم تعمر بالأمس، والمغاني: المنازل التي يعمرها أهلها

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r4.speaker: أهل المعاني
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r4.claim: A broader interpretation says it no longer stood in its former state, encompassing both the land and its produce; the discussion of 'yesterday' continues at 28:19.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p165/r4.anchor: كأن لم تقم على تلك الصفة فيها قبل

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p166/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p166/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p166/r1.claim: Just as this parable has been explained, the Quran's signs are explained for people reflecting on resurrection.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p166/r1.anchor: {كذلك نفصل الآيات} أي: كما بينا هذا المثل للحياة الدنيا

WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p166/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p166/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p166/r2.claim: The flourishing earth seems to promise enjoyment, then the one capable of destroying it returns it to nothing; worldly wealth and beauty likewise gather until death or disaster takes them away, warning against attachment and delusion.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p166/r2.anchor: سلب ذلك عنه بموته أو بحادثة تأتي على ما قد جمعه

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r1.claim: The parable depicts the transient life of this world: rain produces plants eaten by people and livestock until the earth is lush and adorned.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r2.claim: When the landowners expect to harvest and benefit, God's punishment comes by night or day and leaves the land cut down as if it never flourished.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r3.claim: Worldly wealth likewise accumulates and flourishes, then is taken from its owner through death or a disaster that destroys it.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r4.claim: God explains these signs for people who reflect on resurrection.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:10:24/r4.anchor: كما بينا هذا المثل للحياة الدنيا

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:10:24/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:10:24/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:10:24/r1.claim: The verb ihteleta means ‘to mix’; because a plant mixing with water means it absorbs it, the Turkish rendering expresses that result.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:10:24/r1.anchor: Metindeki ihteleta fiili “karışma” anlamına gelir. Bitkinin su ile karışması, –bu bağlamda– bitkinin suyu emmesiyle sonuçlanacağından meâlde bu sonuç dikkate alınmıştır

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:10:24/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:10:24/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:10:24/r2.claim: The transience of worldly beauty, its eventual removal by God, and accountability for earthly deeds are conveyed through a vivid literary simile.
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:10:24/r2.anchor: Dünya hayatındaki güzelliklerin gelip geçici olduğu, onları veren Allah’ın bir gün geri alacağı, dünyada yapıp ettiklerimizin hesabını da öbür dünyada bizden soracağı

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Worldly abundance is temporary: rain makes crops flourish and their owners imagine nobody can take them away, but God can suddenly destroy them.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.anchor: their owners think that who can deprive them of these.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Comfort and luxury do not place a people beyond God’s reach; punishment strikes when they are absorbed in affairs and think no danger is near.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.anchor: it thinks there is no danger for it from around it.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The worldly-life parable continues the previous verse's description of brief worldly benefit: disbelievers are lured by it and imagine it secure and enduring.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.anchor: This is a parable of the life of this world referred to as “benefit from the life of this world for a few days”

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Ikhtilāṭ means intermingling or intertwining and describes lush, dense vegetation produced when conducive rain falls.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.anchor: It signifies the lushness of vegetation and crops. This is because when conducive rain falls on them

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Zayn means embellishment and beauty, came to denote varied vegetation, and the verbs izzayyana and tazayyana convey the same meaning.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.anchor: From here it came to be used for multifarious vegetation.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The parable warns people not to challenge God while intoxicated by comfort: crops and orchards can be ruined suddenly just when owners feel at their peak, as can the deniers.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.anchor: His order to punish them will be given right when they would think that they are in their prime.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Observable signs of sudden ruin invite reflection; a sensible person learns from others' fate before helplessly experiencing punishment himself.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.anchor: Sensible is the person who learns from the fate of others not when he himself helplessly faces it.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Nations facing conclusive communication of truth are seized at their peak because faith and deeds matter more than material resources; resources hasten the fall of a morally bankrupt nation.
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.anchor: the real importance before Him is that of faith and deeds and not of material resources.

TABATABAI:6:74-83#25/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:6:74-83#25/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:6:74-83#25/r1.claim: The Qur’an likens worldly life to vegetation suddenly cut down after flourishing, illustrating why transience should weaken attachment to worldly pleasures.
TABATABAI:6:74-83#25/r1.anchor: حتى إذا أخذت الأرض زخرفها وازينت وظن أهلها أنهم قادرون عليها

BAQILLANI:v1p262/r1.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r1.speaker: بعض أهل الأدب والكلام
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r1.claim: Some literary and theological scholars divide eloquence into ten arts: concision, simile, metaphor, harmony, endings, paronomasia, variation, inclusion, hyperbole, and clarity.
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r1.anchor: ذكر بعض أهل الأدب والكلام أن البلاغة على عشرة أقسام الإيجاز والتشبيه والاستعارة والتلاؤم والفواصل والتجانس والتصريف والتضمين والمبالغة وحسن البيان

BAQILLANI:v1p262/r2.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r2.speaker: author
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r2.claim: Concision conveys many matters in few words without damaging wording or meaning, and comprises omission and brevity.
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r2.anchor: فأما الإيجاز فإنما يحسن مع ترك الإخلال باللفظ والمعنى فيأتي باللفظ القليل الشامل لأمور كثيرة وذلك ينقسم إلى حذف وقصر

BAQILLANI:v1p262/r3.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r3.speaker: author
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r3.claim: Omission can shorten expression; an omitted answer lets the listener infer broadly, as in 'ask the town' and the hypothetical Quran that could move mountains.
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r3.anchor: والحذف أبلغ من الذكر لان النفس تذهب كل مذهب في القصد من الجواب

BAQILLANI:v1p262/r4.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r4.speaker: author
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r4.claim: Brevity by compression is illustrated with Quranic statements about the life-preserving purpose of retaliation, enemies, self-inflicted transgression, and failed plots.
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r4.anchor: والإيجاز بالقصر كقوله ( ﴿ ولكم في القصاص حياة ﴾ )

BAQILLANI:v1p262/r5.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r5.speaker: author
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r5.claim: Simile makes one thing stand in for another in sense or intellect; Bāqillānī includes the worldly-life-and-rain parable among Quranic examples.
BAQILLANI:v1p262/r5.anchor: وأما التشبيه فهو العقد على أن أحد الشيئين يسد مسد الآخر في حس أو عقل

BAQILLANI:v1p172/r1.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r1.speaker: قوم
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r1.claim: Some critics object that the Pleiades cannot be described as presenting themselves in the sky; some explain that the poet meant the setting Jauza instead.
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r1.anchor: قد أنكر عليه قوم قوله إذا ما الثريا في السماء تعرضت وقالوا الثريا لا تتعرض

BAQILLANI:v1p172/r2.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r2.speaker: بعضهم
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r2.claim: A defense says the Pleiades present their broad side as they rise or set, as a sash does when laid out; a cited poem uses the same image of a mare in harness.
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r2.anchor: وقال بعضهم في تصحيح قوله إنما تعرض أول ما تطلع وحين تغرب كما أن الوشاح إذا طرح يلقاك بعرضه

BAQILLANI:v1p172/r3.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r3.speaker: أبو عمرو
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r3.claim: Abu Amr explains the image as the Pleiades crossing the middle of the sky like a sash across a woman's waist.
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r3.anchor: وقال أبو عمرو يعني إذا أخذت الثريا في وسط السماء كما يأخذ الوشاح وسط المرأة

BAQILLANI:v1p172/r4.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r4.speaker: author
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r4.claim: Bāqillānī rejects the objection: the line is among the poem's merits, though other poets also excelled in describing the Pleiades and the poet does not surpass every comparison.
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r4.anchor: والأشبه عندنا أن البيت غير معيب من حيث عابوه به وأنه من محاسن هذه القصيدة

BAQILLANI:v1p172/r5.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r5.speaker: author
BAQILLANI:v1p172/r5.claim: He compares Pleiades imagery by Dhu al-Rumma, Ibn al-Mu'tazz, al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla, and Ibn al-Rumi, including images of a bird's eggs, a silver bridle, and an earring.

BAQILLANI:v1p265/r2.author: al-Bāqillānī
BAQILLANI:v1p265/r2.speaker: author
BAQILLANI:v1p265/r2.claim: Metaphor differs from simile; examples include God's treatment of deeds as scattered dust, the flood and ark, anger falling silent, night stripped from day, truth crushing falsehood, and other vivid Quranic expressions.
BAQILLANI:v1p265/r2.anchor: ومن ذلك & باب الاستعارة & وذلك يباين التشبيه

BURHAN:v1p140/r5.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v1p140/r5.speaker: author
BURHAN:v1p140/r5.claim: من تحتهم occurs in al-Anam, al-Araf, Yunus, and al-Kahf; تجري تحتها الأنهار occurs once in Bara'a.
BURHAN:v1p140/r5.anchor: فى الأنعام والأعراف ويونس والكهف وأما

BURHAN:v3p440/r7.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p440/r7.speaker: author
BURHAN:v3p440/r7.claim: حصيدا borrows the harvested plant for destruction; the shared feature, annihilation, is intellectual.
BURHAN:v3p440/r7.anchor: أصل الحصيد النبات والجامع الهلاك وهو أمر عقلي

BURHAN:v2p140/r4.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v2p140/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURHAN:v2p140/r4.claim: The report that Arabia will again become meadows is linked to the earth’s flourishing before its sudden destruction; the author makes this a sign of the Hour and the world's near end.
BURHAN:v2p140/r4.anchor: وقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم حتى تعود أرض العرب مروجا

BURHAN:v4p208/r2.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v4p208/r2.speaker: author
BURHAN:v4p208/r2.claim: In declarative speech, أو may express doubt, as in the ordinary example “Zayd or ʿAmr came.”
BURHAN:v4p208/r2.anchor: الاول الشك نحو قام زيد أو عمرو

BURHAN:v4p208/r4.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v4p208/r4.speaker: author
BURHAN:v4p208/r4.claim: The “night or day” wording means the command arrives unexpectedly once the earth is adorned and its people feel secure; it does not imply doubt in God.
BURHAN:v4p208/r4.anchor: يريد اذا اخذت الأرض زخرفها واخذ أهلها الامن اتاها امرنا وهم لايعلمون أي فجأة فهذا ابهام لان الشك محال على الله تعالى

BURHAN:v4p336/r7.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v4p336/r7.speaker: author
BURHAN:v4p336/r7.claim: A lām in a لو response can signal that the severe outcome is delayed, as in the adorned earth’s sudden destruction; omitting it can suggest immediate change, as with making water bitter.
BURHAN:v4p336/r7.anchor: والمسبوقة في جواب لو كقوله تعالى

BURHAN:v4p336/r8.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v4p336/r8.speaker: author
BURHAN:v4p336/r8.claim: An oath-signaling lām may enter a conditional particle after an oath stated or understood, marking the following answer as belonging to the oath rather than the condition.
BURHAN:v4p336/r8.anchor: والمؤذنة الداخلة على أداة الشرط بعد تقدم القسم لفظا أو تقديرا

BURHAN:v2p93/r1.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v2p93/r1.speaker: النظام
BURHAN:v2p93/r1.claim: Al-Nazzam holds that the Arabs could have matched the Quran, but God diverted them and stripped away their ability through an external impediment.
BURHAN:v2p93/r1.anchor: وهو قول النظام ( 2 ) إن الله صرف العرب عن معارضته

BURHAN:v2p93/r2.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v2p93/r2.speaker: author
BURHAN:v2p93/r2.claim: The challenge says humans and jinn cannot produce a like of the Quran even when united, which indicates their inability while their powers remain; otherwise the challenge would be pointless.
BURHAN:v2p93/r2.anchor: فإنه يدل على عجزهم مع بقاء قدرتهم ولو سئلوا القدرة

BURHAN:v2p93/r3.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v2p93/r3.speaker: author
BURHAN:v2p93/r3.claim: The doctrine of diversion wrongly transfers the miracle from the Quran to God's removal of people's ability, despite consensus that the Quran itself is the enduring supreme miracle.
BURHAN:v2p93/r3.anchor: هذا مع أن الإجماع منعقد على إضافة الإعجاز إلى القرآن

BURHAN:v2p93/r4.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v2p93/r4.speaker: author
BURHAN:v2p93/r4.claim: If diversion ended with the challenge period, the Quran would cease to be miraculous; that contradicts the consensus that the Prophet's supreme miracle remains and that the Quran is his only enduring miracle.
BURHAN:v2p93/r4.anchor: وأيضا يلزم من القول بالصرفة فساد آخر وهو زوال الإعجاز بزوال زمان التحدي

BURHAN:v2p93/r5.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v2p93/r5.speaker: القاضي أبو بكر
BURHAN:v2p93/r5.claim: Qadi Abu Bakr argues that if matching were possible but blocked by diversion, the speech would not itself be miraculous; the blocking would be the miracle, leaving no intrinsic superiority in the Quran.
BURHAN:v2p93/r5.anchor: قال القاضي أبو بكر ( 2 ) ( ومما يبطل القول بالصرفة

BURHAN:v2p93/r6.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v2p93/r6.speaker: فريق منهم
BURHAN:v2p93/r6.claim: One group claims everyone can produce a Quranic counterpart but lacks knowledge of its arrangement; if they learned that arrangement, they could reach it.
BURHAN:v2p93/r6.anchor: وليس هذا بأعجب مما ذهب إليه فريق منهم أن الكل قادرون

BURHAN:v2p93/r7.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v2p93/r7.speaker: فريق منهم
BURHAN:v2p93/r7.claim: Another group claims human and divine speech do not differ in this respect and that either can be inimitable on the same basis.
BURHAN:v2p93/r7.anchor: ولا بأعجب من قول فريق منهم إنه لا فرق بين كلام البشر وكلام الله

BURHAN:v2p93/r8.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v2p93/r8.speaker: قوم
BURHAN:v2p93/r8.claim: Some allege that Ibn al-Muqaffa opposed the Quran, although what he wrote was only maxims.
BURHAN:v2p93/r8.anchor: وزعم قوم أن ابن المقفع عارض القرآن وإنما وضع حكما

BURHAN:v2p93/r9.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v2p93/r9.speaker: author
BURHAN:v2p93/r9.claim: The author locates inimitability in the Quran's distinctive composition: its words are balanced in arrangement and meter, and its compound expressions reach the highest level of meaning and expression.
BURHAN:v2p93/r9.anchor: الثاني أن وجه الإعجاز راجع إلى التأليف الخاص به لا مطلق التأليف

BURHAN:v3p420/r1.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p420/r1.speaker: author
BURHAN:v3p420/r1.claim: Similes may join two sensory things, two rational things, or render an abstract meaning sensory; examples include the old date stalk, stone-like hearts, spiders, ash, and the donkey carrying scripture.
BURHAN:v3p420/r1.anchor: ينقسم باعتبار طرفيه إلى أربعة أقسام لأنهما

BURHAN:v3p420/r3.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p420/r3.speaker: الإمام
BURHAN:v3p420/r3.claim: The Imam bars comparing a sensory thing to an intellectual one because intellect is derived from sensation; making the derivative the original would reverse their order.
BURHAN:v3p420/r3.anchor: أما عكسه فمنعه الإمام لأن العقل مستفاد من الحس

BURHAN:v3p420/r4.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p420/r4.speaker: غيره
BURHAN:v3p420/r4.claim: Other scholars allow the reverse comparison, illustrated by a poem likening stars amid dark to established Sunnahs among innovations.

BURHAN:v3p420/r7.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p420/r7.speaker: author
BURHAN:v3p420/r7.claim: The extraordinary is brought into familiar experience: the raised mountain resembles a canopy, while worldly life resembles rain-fed growth through its beauty, adornment, subsequent ruin, and lesson.
BURHAN:v3p420/r7.anchor: والجامع البهجة والزينة ثم الهلاك وفيه العبرة

BURHAN:v3p306/r1.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p306/r1.speaker: ابن الضائع
BURHAN:v3p306/r1.claim: Ibn al-Da'i objects that the grammatical usage under discussion can properly apply to God; the author calls this a grave error.
BURHAN:v3p306/r1.anchor: ورد عليه ابن الضائع بصحة وقوعها على الله عز وجل قال وهذا غاية الخطأ

BURHAN:v3p102/r1.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p102/r1.speaker: author
BURHAN:v3p102/r1.claim: Ellipsis linguistically means removal; technically it is omitting part or all of a statement where evidence supports the omission. Calling omission without evidence اقتصار is imprecise because nothing is actually omitted.
BURHAN:v3p102/r1.anchor: واصطلاحا إسقاط جزء الكلام أو كله لدليل وأما قول النحويين الحذف لغير دليل ويسمى اقتصارا فلا تحرير فيه

BURHAN:v3p102/r4.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p102/r4.speaker: author
BURHAN:v3p102/r4.claim: The roots distinguish concealment from cutting away: إضمار hides an element, whereas حذف suggests removing and discarding it, which explains the grammatical contrast between overt and implicit forms.

BURHAN:v3p102/r5.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p102/r5.speaker: ابن ميمون
BURHAN:v3p102/r5.claim: Ibn Maymun rejects saying that a subject is deleted in the verbal-noun construction; he says it is implicit because the subject is an essential part of speech.
BURHAN:v3p102/r5.anchor: ورد ابن ميمون قول النحاة إن الفاعل

BURHAN:v3p102/r6.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p102/r6.speaker: ابن جنى
BURHAN:v3p102/r6.claim: Ibn Jinni says an understood subject attached to a verb, as in قم, is implicit rather than deleted; he rejects al-Kisa'i's analysis in ضربني وضربت قومك.
BURHAN:v3p102/r6.anchor: وقال ابن جنى في خاطرياته من اتصال الفاعل بالفعل

BURHAN:v4p81/r1.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v4p81/r1.speaker: author
BURHAN:v4p81/r1.claim: The author distinguishes جاء, used when the arrival is visible or as if witnessed, from أتى for the unseen crops/earth; thus the earth's command comes as أتاها, while the visible command is جاء.

BURHAN:v4p81/r5.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v4p81/r5.speaker: author
BURHAN:v4p81/r5.claim: عمل is narrower than فعل: every عمل is a فعل, but not every فعل is عمل; عمل involves duration or repetition, whereas فعل is more general.
BURHAN:v4p81/r5.anchor: والفرق بينهما إن العمل اخص من الفعل كل عمل فعل

BURHAN:v3p290/r2.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p290/r2.speaker: الفارسي
BURHAN:v3p290/r2.claim: Al-Fārisī also includes the phrasing about vegetation mixing with the rain among examples of this construction.

ITQAN:v3p115/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v3p115/r1.speaker: author
ITQAN:v3p115/r1.claim: Similes fall into four types by whether their two sides are both sensory, both rational, or one of each.
ITQAN:v3p115/r1.anchor: الأول باعتبار طرفيه إلى أربعة أقسام لأنهما إما حسيان أو عقليان أو المشبه به حسي والمشبه عقلي

ITQAN:v3p115/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v3p115/r5.speaker: الإمام
ITQAN:v3p115/r5.claim: The Imam rejects comparison in which a sensory subject is likened to a rational one, since reason derives from sense; that would make the source subordinate to what derives from it.
ITQAN:v3p115/r5.anchor: ومثال الرابع لم يقع في القرآن بل منعه الإمام أصلا لأن العقل مستفاد من الحس فالمحسوس أصل للمعقول

ITQAN:v3p115/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v3p115/r8.speaker: author
ITQAN:v3p115/r8.claim: The ten-clause water simile as a whole captures worldly life’s swift passing, fading enjoyment, and people’s deluded confidence: lush growth suddenly disappears at God’s command.
ITQAN:v3p115/r8.anchor: فإن فيه عشر جمل وقع التركيب من مجموعها بحيث لو سقط منها شيء اختل التشبيه إذ المقصود تشبيه حال الدنيا في سرعة تقضيها وانقراض نعيمها واغترار الناس بها

ITQAN:v3p115/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v3p115/r9.speaker: author
ITQAN:v3p115/r9.claim: One explanation of the water comparison is that taking more water than needed harms, while taking only what is needed benefits—like worldly life.
ITQAN:v3p115/r9.anchor: وقال بعضهم وجه تشبيه الدنيا بالماء أمران أحدهما أن الماء إذا أخذت منه فوق حاجتك تضررت وإن أخذت قدر الحاجة انتفعت به

ITQAN:v3p120#2/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v3p120#2/r1.speaker: author
ITQAN:v3p120#2/r1.claim: Metaphor has three pillars: the borrowed expression, the source meaning from which it is borrowed, and the shared meaning joining source and target.
ITQAN:v3p120#2/r1.anchor: أركان الاستعارة ثلاثة مستعار وهو لفظ المشبه به ومستعار منه وهو معنى اللفظ المشبه ومستعار له

ITQAN:v3p120#2/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v3p120#2/r3.speaker: ابن أبي الإصبع
ITQAN:v3p120#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abi al-Isba calls metaphor from perceptible to perceptible through an intellectual feature subtler; here harvested vegetation evokes destruction, an intellectual common feature.
ITQAN:v3p120#2/r3.anchor: قال ابن أبي الإصبع وهي ألطف من الأولى

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r1.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r1.claim: Verbal nouns and active participles are not overt sentences, but retain sentence force because they work like verbs and take complements accordingly.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r1.anchor: المصدر واسم الفاعل ليسا بجملتين صريحا ولكن حكم الجملة قائم فيهما

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r2.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r2.claim: A true parable is an extended, non-obvious comparison extracted from one or more sentences; the more purely intellectual the likeness, the more sentence-level context it needs.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r2.anchor: المثل الحقيقي والتشبيه الذي هو الأولى بأن يسمى تمثيلا لبعده عن التشبيه الظاهر الصريح

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r3.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r3.claim: The worldly-life parable in 10:24 contains ten sentences when separated, and its likeness comes from their inseparable whole; deleting any one harms the point.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r3.anchor: حتى إنك ترى في هذه الآية عشر جمل إذا فصلت وهي وإن كان قد دخل بعضها في بعض

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r4.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r4.claim: Count linked, sequential clauses as the units of an extended parable; do not confuse them with independent comparisons whose order can freely change.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p86/r4.anchor: ولا ينبغي أن تعد الجمل في هذا النحو بعد التشبيهات التى يضم بعضها إلى بعض

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r1.speaker: النبي
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r1.claim: The Prophet likens people to a hundred camels among which one can scarcely find a rideable mount.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r1.anchor: بيان هذا أن قول النبي الناس كإبل مائة لا تكاد تجد فيها راحلة

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r2.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r2.claim: Some parables require keeping the image bearer because the following clause cannot be shifted onto the subject being compared.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r2.anchor: لا بد فيه من المحافظة على ذكر المشبه به الذي هو الإبل فلو قلت الناس لا تجد فيهم راحلة

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r3.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r3.claim: In 10:24 water must remain the image bearer: the actions narrated of water cannot sensibly be predicated of worldly life.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r3.anchor: لو أردت أن تحذف الماء الذي هو المشبه به وتنقل الكلام إلى المشبه الذي هو الحياة

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r4.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r4.claim: A clause after the image bearer may be a relative clause, an adjective of an indefinite image, or an independent sentence after a definite image, as in 2:17 and 29:41.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p91/r4.anchor: والجملة إذا جاءت بعد المشبه به لم تخل من ثلاثة أوجه

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r1.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r1.claim: Deleting the simile particle can leave an estimated مثل in the underlying syntax, as in the phrase you are like the night and the expression ask the village.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r1.anchor: تجعل الأصل فإنك مثل الليل ثم تحذف مثلا

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r2.speaker: النبي
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r2.claim: The Prophet compares a believer to a tender grain stalk and people to a hundred camels with few rideable mounts; Jurjani uses both to explain particle deletion.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r2.anchor: في قول النبي مثل المؤمن مثل الخامة من الزرع المؤمن الخامة من الزرع

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r3.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r3.claim: With a simple image such as Zayd is a lion, deleting the particle intensifies likeness toward identity; with a descriptive clause, the omitted مثل preserves an ordinary simile.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r3.anchor: أنك إذا حذفت الكاف هناك فقلت زيد الأسد

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r4.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r4.claim: Calling a person the night is not the aim when the point is night reaching everywhere; the clause specifies the likeness rather than making the person night.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r4.anchor: وبعيد أن تقول جعله الليل لأن القصد لم يقع إلى وصف في الليل كالظلمة ونحوها

JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r5.speaker: author
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r5.claim: The water parable diagnoses the difference: deleting water and saying worldly life is water gives no sensible reading unless مثل is understood as omitted.
JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p214/r5.anchor: لو قلت إنما الحياة الدنيا ماء أنزلناه من السماء أو الماء ينزل من السماء

RUMMANI:v1p82/r6.author: al-Rummānī
RUMMANI:v1p82/r6.speaker: author
RUMMANI:v1p82/r6.claim: The simile joins the world's beauty and flourishing to its subsequent destruction, teaching that everything perishable is insignificant however long-lived or great it seems.
RUMMANI:v1p82/r6.anchor: إنما مثل الحياة الدنيا كماء أنزلناه من السماء فاختلط به نبات الأرض

RUMMANI:v1p91/r10.author: al-Rummānī
RUMMANI:v1p91/r10.speaker: author
RUMMANI:v1p91/r10.claim: حصيدا literally describes vegetation cut down; its metaphor for a ruined settlement is stronger because it invokes something visible to the eye.
RUMMANI:v1p91/r10.anchor: {أتاها أمرنا ليلا أو نهارا فجعلناها حصيدا كأن لم تغن بالأمس}

DAMGHANI:v1p215/r9.author: al-Dāmghānī
DAMGHANI:v1p215/r9.speaker: author
DAMGHANI:v1p215/r9.claim: Zukhruf can mean beauty: the earth takes on its beauty and adornment.
DAMGHANI:v1p215/r9.anchor: الثاني : الزخرف الحسن قوله تعالى في سورة يونس

DAMGHANI:v1p223/r1.author: al-Dāmghānī
DAMGHANI:v1p223/r1.speaker: author
DAMGHANI:v1p223/r1.claim: Zīna can mean the earth’s red, yellow, and green coloration.
DAMGHANI:v1p223/r1.anchor: الزينة التلون الأحمر والأصفر والأخضر قوله تعالى في سورة يونس

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p335#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p335#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p335#2/r1.claim: Zukhruf originally means ornament and beautification; it can name anything used to adorn or speech embellished with lies.
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p335#2/r1.anchor: الأصل في الزخرف : الزينة والتحسين ، يقال زخرف يزخرف زخرفة

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p335#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p335#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p335#2/r3.claim: In this verse zukhruf means the earth's beauty or full adornment.
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p335#2/r3.anchor: والثاني : الحسن . ومنه قوله تعالى في يونس

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r1.claim: For ka-an lam yagh naw fīhā, she prefers as though they had not inhabited it over as though they had never existed; the former better fits the contextual sense.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r1.anchor: تأويل {كَأَنْ لَمْ يَغْنَوْا فِيهَا} في (وق) : كأن لم يعمروا، أوْلَى من: كأن لم يكونوا.

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r2.speaker: ابن الأثير
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r2.claim: Ibn al-Athīr glosses ghaniya bi-l-makān as staying or residing, citing a saying attributed to ʿAlī about not spending a full day safely in learning.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r2.anchor: وإليه دهب ابن الأثير في حديث عليًّ كرم الله وجهه: "ورجل سماه الناس عالماً ولم يغن في العلم يوماً سالماً" قال: أي لم يلبث

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r3.speaker: الراغب
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r3.claim: Al-Rāghib connects dwelling in a place with the root’s sense of sufficiency: remaining there a long time, self-sufficient and needing nothing else.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r3.anchor: على أن بين (لم يغنوا) ولم يعمروا أو لم يقيموا، فرقا دقيقا في الدلالة، التفت إليه "الراغب" حين ربط الغنى في المكان

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r4.claim: She adds that Qur’anic ghaniya bi-l-makān occurs only in negative descriptions of ruined peoples and worldly life, exposing the illusion that any worldly dwelling provides lasting sufficiency.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r4.anchor: ولم تأت الكلمة في القرآن إلا منفية، في خبر ديار ثمود ومدين، ومثل الحياة الدنيا

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r5.claim: Poetic attestations by Muhalhil and Labīd explicitly support the sense of inhabiting or dwelling, which bare glosses such as remaining do not fully convey.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p484/r5.anchor: وهو لا يفيد معنى التعمير وهو صريح في الشاهدين لمهلهل ولبيد

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r1.claim: Arabic speakers differ in eloquence; Qur’anic inimitability does not require every individual to think they can reproduce it, nor does it depend on collective inability alone.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r1.anchor: الفصحى أن العرب الفصحاء ليسوا سواء في المقدرة البيانية والمرتبة البلاغية.

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r2.claim: As a miracle, Qur’anic eloquence was recognizable by every native Arabic speaker, not only the most gifted rhetoricians; al-Bāqillānī confuses this recognition with the separate challenge.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r2.anchor: فمن حيث هو معجز. الأمر فيه واضح لكل ذي سليقة عربية أصلية.

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r3.claim: The challenge to compose a comparable sura is a separate demand addressed to the most eloquent speakers and their alleged jinn allies.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r3.anchor: وأما من حيث تحديهم أن يأتوا بسورة من مثله، فتلك قضية أخرى معروضة على أبلغ بلغائهم

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r4.claim: She compares recognition and challenge to poetry: ordinary listeners appreciate or reject a poem, while only fellow poets attempt to rival it.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r4.anchor: كان يقول قصيدته فيتلقاها جمهور المستمعين بالإعجاب والتقدير أو الصد والتهاون

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r5.claim: Quraysh sought to divert all Arab pilgrims from hearing the Qur’an, not just eloquent specialists, because pure Arabic speakers naturally sensed and distinguished its language.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p45/r5.anchor: لم يكونوا يتحرون الخطباء البلغاء والشعراء الفحول منهم أو يُقدرون أن الوافدين على الموسم كانوا سواء

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r1.claim: The situation directs the challenge to those who believe they can match the Qur’an, just as Moses’ sign confronted Pharaoh’s most skilled magicians.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r1.anchor: وموسى عليه السلام، عاجز بآيته قوم فرعون، فندب له أمهر السحرة في زمانه.

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r2.claim: The commands to summon helpers imply that Quraysh should call those they considered capable rivals to produce a comparable Qur’an.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r2.anchor: ويؤنس إلى تعلق التحدي بأبلغ بلغائهم قوله تعالى في آيتي التحدي، من سورتى يونس وهود:

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r3.speaker: الباقلاني
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r3.claim: Bint accepts al-Bāqillānī’s point that eloquence varies among people, while retaining the distinction between elite challenge and universal recognition of the miracle.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r3.anchor: وفي هذا يقبل ما ذكره الباقلانى من تفاوت مراتبهم في البلاغة

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r4.speaker: الباقلاني وفريق من المتكلمين
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r4.claim: She rejects claims that everyone could match the Qur’an if they knew its arrangement, or that human and divine speech are equally capable of inimitability.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r4.anchor: ونعجب مع الباقلانى لمن "ذهب إلى أن الكل قادرون على الإتيان بمثله، وإنما يتأخرون عنه لعدم العلم بوجه ترتيب

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r5.claim: She says theologians imposed these theories on the challenge; even Quraysh, while claiming human authorship, did not think their best rhetoricians could imitate the Qur’an.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r5.anchor: ونراها مما أقحمه بعض المتكلمين على قضية التحدي، فكا خطر على بال المشركين حين تورطوا جدلاً

BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r6.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r6.speaker: author
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r6.claim: The Qur’an challenges jinn alongside humans; she relates this to the Arab belief that every master poet had a jinn companion who inspired exceptional verse.
BINTSHATI-IJAZ:p70/r6.anchor: والقرآن يتحدى الجن مع الإنس. ونفهم من معاجزة الجن، ما تواترت به المرويات من أن العرب كان الشعر يبهرها

SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH:p104/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH:p104/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH:p104/r1.claim: Against Orientalist criticism based on differing versions of Moses’ story, the same scene can be expressed in many ways, but their rhetorical artistry is unequal and no wording matches the Quran.
SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH:p104/r1.anchor: القصة الواحدة في القرآن قد يُعبّر عنها بصور مختلفة لكن اختيار الصورة المعجزة هو اختيار القرآن الكريم

SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH:p104/r2.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH:p104/r2.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH:p104/r2.claim: The Quran gives an exact, artistically miraculous rendering of what prophets meant; Moses had difficulty expressing himself and asked for Aaron, who was more eloquent.
SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH:p104/r2.anchor: لأن موسى كان في لسانه عجمة (ولا يكاد يُبين) كما جاء على لسان فرعون

SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH:p104/r3.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH:p104/r3.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH:p104/r3.claim: The inimitability challenge applies even to a very short surah such as al-Kawthar, whose eloquent choices cannot be reproduced.
SAMARRAI-ASRAR-MUH:p104/r3.anchor: فلا يمكن صياغة سورة مثل سور القرآن الكريم حتى لو كان المحتوى

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p1007/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p1007/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p1007/r1.claim: The ornament belongs to the earth and what grows on it; flowers and other beauty delight viewers, as God's adornment of the sky does.
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p1007/r1.anchor: فالزينة هي للأرض والله تعالى قال (حَتَّىَ إِذَا أَخَذَتِ

NASHR:v1p334/r1.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p334/r1.speaker: author
NASHR:v1p334/r1.claim: He takes both options for Hafs through Amr al-Sabbah and Hisham through al-Hulwani, relying on the Iraqi routes’ established transmission of short madd.
NASHR:v1p334/r1.anchor: عن حفص من طريق عمرو بن الصباح

NASHR:v1p334/r2.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p334/r2.speaker: author
NASHR:v1p334/r2.claim: For al-Asbahani from Warsh he takes both lengths, as for Qalun: both are explicitly transmitted, although short madd is more famous; he does not mix unestablished routes.
NASHR:v1p334/r2.anchor: لثبوت الوجهين جميعا عنه نصا كما ذكرنا من الأئمة

NASHR:v1p334/r3.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p334/r3.speaker: author
NASHR:v1p334/r3.claim: He uses full, unexaggerated madd in both categories for Hamza, Warsh through al-Azraq, and Ibn Dhakwan through al-Akhfash.
NASHR:v1p334/r3.anchor: لحمزة وورش من طريق الأزرق على السواء

NASHR:v1p334/r4.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p334/r4.speaker: author
NASHR:v1p334/r4.claim: For readers who lengthen separated madd by an intermediate degree, he also uses an intermediate degree in connected madd for all readers who otherwise shorten it.
NASHR:v1p334/r4.anchor: لسائر القراء ممن مد المنفصل بالتوسط في المرتبتين

NASHR:v1p334/r5.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p334/r5.speaker: author
NASHR:v1p334/r5.claim: In his graded scheme, short separated madd belongs to Ibn Kathir, Abu Jafar, and disputed readers such as Qalun and Abu Amr; connected madd rises slightly for the short-madd group.
NASHR:v1p334/r5.anchor: كابن كثير وأبي جعفر وأصحاب الخلاف كقالون وأبي عمرو

NASHR:v1p334/r6.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p334/r6.speaker: author
NASHR:v1p334/r6.claim: His next degrees rise slightly for al-Kisai, Khalaf, and Ibn Amir, then Asim, then Hamza, Warsh, and al-Akhfash from Ibn Dhakwan’s Iraqi route; only those who pause on madd exceed them.
NASHR:v1p334/r6.anchor: ثم فوقها قليلا للكسائي وخلف ولابن عامر

NASHR:v1p334/r7.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p334/r7.speaker: author
NASHR:v1p334/r7.claim: He allows graded lengths in both madd categories or only separated madd; under the latter method connected madd stays uniformly full, and he generally chooses the majority position on necessary madd.
NASHR:v1p334/r7.anchor: فإن مراتبه عندي في المنفصل كما ذكرت آنفا

NASHR:v2p205/r1.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v2p205/r1.speaker: author
NASHR:v2p205/r1.claim: He varied the order while gathering readings with Abu al-Maali ibn al-Labban because that teacher had exceptional recall; this flexible method suits only similarly capable pupils.
NASHR:v2p205/r1.anchor: وكنت أنوع بمثل هذه التنويعات حالة الجمع على أبي المعالي بن اللبان لأنه كان أقوى من لقيت استحضارا

NASHR:v2p205/r2.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v2p205/r2.speaker: author
NASHR:v2p205/r2.claim: A pupil with weaker recall should follow one fixed sequence, which makes the material easier to retrieve and retain.
NASHR:v2p205/r2.anchor: أما من كان ضعيفا في الاستحضار فينبغي أن يسلك به نوعا واحدا من الترتيب لا يزول عنه

NASHR:v2p205/r3.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v2p205/r3.speaker: الناس
NASHR:v2p205/r3.claim: Many readers start with Qalun because the famous manuals place him first.
NASHR:v2p205/r3.anchor: وكثير من الناس يرى تقديم قالون

NASHR:v2p205/r4.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v2p205/r4.speaker: author
NASHR:v2p205/r4.claim: Others begin with Warsh through al-Azraq because his many distinctive modes make it practical to start with long madd, then medium, then short; this is the author’s choice.

NASHR:v2p205/r5.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v2p205/r5.speaker: author
NASHR:v2p205/r5.claim: When using a fixed sequence, he learned only the order taught by his teachers: after Warsh through al-Azraq come al-Asbahani, Qalun, Abu Jafar, Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Yaqub, Ibn Amir, Asim, Hamza, al-Kisai, and Khalaf.

NASHR:v2p205/r6.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v2p205/r6.speaker: author
NASHR:v2p205/r6.claim: In ordered reading, complete each reader before moving on, starting with the narrator listed first for each teacher; experienced teachers stopped premature transitions to prevent omissions.
NASHR:v2p205/r6.anchor: ولا ينتقل إلى من بعده حتى يكمل من قبل

NASHR:v2p205/r7.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v2p205/r7.speaker: بعض شيوخنا
NASHR:v2p205/r7.claim: Some teachers gently tapped the ground to prompt a reader to notice what he had missed, then waited or told him he had not yet reached that point.
NASHR:v2p205/r7.anchor: يضرب بيده الأرض خفيفا ليتفطن القارئ ما فاته

NASHR:v2p205/r8.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v2p205/r8.speaker: بعض الشيوخ
NASHR:v2p205/r8.claim: Other teachers let the pupil finish the faces he thought complete before telling him he had not yet finished.
NASHR:v2p205/r8.anchor: حتى يكمل الأوجه في زعمه وينتقل في القراءة إلى ما بعد

NASHR:v1p398/r1.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p398/r1.speaker: author
NASHR:v1p398/r1.claim: For the preceding hamza-substitution case, between-between easing is more common than replacement and is the majority reading.
NASHR:v1p398/r1.anchor: بين بين في هذا أكثر وأشهر

NASHR:v1p398/r2.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p398/r2.speaker: الكسائي والباقون
NASHR:v1p398/r2.claim: Al-Kisai deletes the hamza throughout the preceding set, while the other readers retain it.
NASHR:v1p398/r2.anchor: الكسائي بحذف الهمزة في ذلك كله

NASHR:v1p398/r5.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p398/r5.speaker: author
NASHR:v1p398/r5.claim: Al-Asbahani from Warsh eases both hamzas in every form of كأن, including كأن لم تغن and forms with doubled or light nūn.
NASHR:v1p398/r5.anchor: وكذلك الهمزتين من " كأن " كيف أتت، مشددة أم مخففة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r1.speaker: المعتزلة
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r1.claim: The Muʿtazila agree that God’s being a speaker means He creates speech, with no real attribute accruing to Him, and that divine speech is created, composed of letters and sounds.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r1.anchor: أما المعتزلة فاتفقوا كافة على أن معنى كونه تعالى متكلما أنه خالق الكلام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r2.speaker: الجبائي وأبو هاشم
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r2.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī and his son Abū Hāshim hold that divine speech is originated in a locus.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r2.anchor: الجبائي وإبنه أبو هاشم إلى أنه حادث في محل

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r3.speaker: الجبائي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r3.claim: Al-Jubbāʾī further says God creates speech for Himself at each reciter’s place of recitation; the other Muʿtazilites disagree.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r3.anchor: يحدث عند قراءة كل قاريء كلاما لنفسه في محل القراءة وخالفه الباقون

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r4.speaker: أبو الهذيل بن العلاف
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r4.claim: Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf and his followers place some divine speech in a locus, such as “Be,” while commands, prohibitions, reports, and questions are not in a locus.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r4.anchor: وذهب أبو الهذيل بن العلاف وأصحابه إلى أن بعضه في محل وهو قوله كن وبعضه لا في محل

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r5.speaker: الحسن بن محمد النجار
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r5.claim: Al-Ḥasan b. Muḥammad al-Najjār says God’s speech is an accident when recited and a body when written.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r5.anchor: الحسن بن محمد النجار إلى ان كلام الباري إذا قريء فهو عرض وإذا كتب فهو جسم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r6.speaker: الإمامية والخوارج والحشوية
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r6.claim: The Imāmiyya, Khārijites, and Ḥashwiyya also describe divine speech as composed of letters and sounds, though they differ on its status.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r6.anchor: وذهبت الإمامية والخوارج والحشوية إلى أن كلام الرب تعالى مركب من الحروف والأصوات

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r7.speaker: الحشوية
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r7.claim: The Ḥashwiyya regard the letter-and-sound speech as eternal and subsisting in God; some make it like human speech, while others distinguish eternal from originated letters and sounds.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r7.anchor: لكن منهم من زعم أنه من جنس كلام البشر

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r8.speaker: الكرامية
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r8.claim: The Karrāmiyya say “speech” means either the capacity to speak, which is eternal and singular, or utterances, which are temporal and multiple; both subsist in God.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r8.anchor: وأما الكرامية فقالوا إن الكلام قد يطلق على القدرة على التكلم وقد يطلق على الأقوال والعبارات

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r9.speaker: الواقفية
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r9.claim: The Wāqifiyya agree that divine speech came to be after not existing, but differ over whether to call it eternal or created; some avoid “created” while calling it originated.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r9.anchor: وأما الواقفية فقد أجمعوا على أن كلام الرب تعالى كائن بعد أن لم يكن

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r10.speaker: بعض القائلين بالحدوث
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r10.claim: Some who hold divine speech originated say it is neither a substance nor an accident.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r10.anchor: ومن القائلين بالحدوث من قال ليس جوهرا ولا عرضا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r11.speaker: بعض المعترفين بالصانع
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r11.claim: Some who acknowledge a Creator deny that He can be described as speaking, whether by speech or without speech.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r11.anchor: وذهب بعض المعترفين بالصانع إلى أنه لا يوصف بكونه متكلما لا بكلام ولا بغير كلام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r12.claim: The dispute arises from two apparently conflicting syllogisms: speech is God’s attribute and attributes are eternal, but ordered successive letters are temporal.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r12.anchor: وكل ما هو صفة له فهو قديم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r13.claim: One camp makes God’s letter-and-sound speech eternal and denies that every composition of letters and sounds must be temporal; al-Ālūsī says false claims have been attributed to them.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r13.anchor: فقوم ذهبوا إلى أن كلامه تعالى حروف وأصوات وهي قديمة ومنعوا أن كل ما هو مؤلف من حروف وأصوات فهو حادث

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r14.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r14.claim: Another camp treats speech as temporal sounds and letters subsisting in another locus, such as a tablet or Gabriel, and defines God as speaker by His producing them there.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r14.anchor: وآخرون قالوا بحدوث كلامه تعالى وأنه مؤلف من أصوات وحروف وهو قائم بغيره

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r15.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r15.claim: A further camp makes speech a temporal attribute of God composed of letters and sounds, denying that every attribute of God must be eternal.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r15.anchor: واللغة ذهبوا إلى أن كلامه تعالى صفة له مؤلفة من الحروف والأصوات

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r16.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r16.claim: Another group says divine speech is one simple meaning subsisting in God and denies that it is composed of letters and sounds.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r16.anchor: كلامه تعالى معنى واحد بسيط قائم بذاته تعالى فهم منعوا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r17.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r17.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r17.claim: Some thinkers, overwhelmed by the dispute, suspend judgment and leave the matter unresolved.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r17.anchor: وبعضهم تحير فوقف وحبس ذهنه في مسجد الدهشة واعتكف

ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r18.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r18.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r18.claim: Al-Ālūsī says both syllogisms are sound and both conclusions true, since different circumstances call for different accounts of speech.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p19/r18.anchor: وعندي القياسان صحيحان والنتيجتان صادقتان ولكل مقام مقال ولكل كلام أحوال

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r1.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports that a Qurʾan reciter who regularly reviews it resembles someone tending tethered camels: he retains them, but if he releases them they escape; the report is in Muslim and al-Nasāʾī.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r1.anchor: عن ابن عمر؛ أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: " إنما مثل صاحب القرآن كمثل صاحب الإبل المعقلة

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r2.claim: Ibn Kathīr corrects Ibn al-Jawzī’s claim that the ʿAbd al-Razzāq route is in both Ṣaḥīḥs: it is unique to Muslim.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r2.anchor: قاله (4) ابن الجوزي في جامع المسانيد، وإنما هو من أفراد مسلم من حديث عبد الرزاق

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r3.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reports the Prophet’s warning not to say “I forgot such-and-such a verse” but that one was made to forget it; review the Qurʾan, which escapes people’s hearts faster than camels. Al-Tirmidhī grades the report ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r3.anchor: عن شقيق: سمعت عبد الله قال: سمعت النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r4.speaker: النسائي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r4.claim: Most routes from Manṣūr raise the report to the Prophet, but al-Nasāʾī also transmits it from ʿAbd Allāh as a Companion statement; Ibn Kathīr calls that stopped route unusual.
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p70#2/r4.anchor: وقد رواه النسائي عن قتيبة، عن حماد بن زيد، عن منصور، عن أبي وائل، عن عبد الله موقوفا
